AlphaGenome in-silico shuffling of AP-1 (Fos) sites: cardiomyocyte arm

Generated 21 Oct 2026 · 3,679 cardiomyocyte Fos sites, 10 shuffle replicates per width · mouse heart ATAC track · fibroblast arm and MPRA still running

Main takeaways
  • What is solid. Shuffling the 170 bp around an AP-1 site removes far more predicted accessibility (median log2FC -1.75 in Stable sites) than shuffling the 11 bp motif alone (-0.61). This holds for essentially every site and is well above replicate noise.
  • Stable vs Dynamic is real. Stable sites depend more on their 170 bp context than Dynamic sites (+0.52, 95% CI +0.41 to +0.62). It survives adjustment for native accessibility and peak width, stratification by accessibility, a permutation test, and a second independent track (smaller there).
  • Age vs exercise vs combination. All dynamic classes behave alike. Comparing classes with each other (Age Up vs Down, Exercise Up vs Down) finds no differences at 170 bp or peak level. What separates classes is being stably bound or not, not the direction of change.
  • What is noise or unusable. RNA effects are about zero; AP-1 motif insertion into random backgrounds is at the floor; per-site peak-shuffle values scatter widely (replicate SD about 0.6) and are only trustworthy in aggregate.
  • New in this version. Data QC (Part A) shows the class labels are directionally real in independent snATAC, the model reproduces the slides' Dynamic-site values, shuffles behave as intended, 10 replicates are justified and GPU type does not matter. Further analyses (Part C) show that dependence on the 170 bp context grows with distance from a TSS and with TOBIAS footprint strength, that sites rarely depend on the motif alone, that two motifs in one peak do not buffer each other, and that AlphaGenome's predicted shuffle effects do not track the fibroblast MPRA (rho ≈ 0).
  • Caveat on the slides. Our Dynamic-site native accessibility matches the slides closely, which suggests the pipeline reproduces the API, but our Stable-site set differs from the slides' (we could not reproduce their site counts). Absolute numbers should not be compared directly with the slides until the site set is resolved.

How to read this report

Effect. For each site and shuffle width, the effect is the mean over 10 shuffles of log2((shuffled + pc) / (native + pc)) of the predicted ATAC (mean per-base signal over a region; pc = 5% of the median native value). Negative = accessibility lost. A shuffle of the motif is read out over the motif, a 170 bp shuffle over the 170 bp, a peak shuffle over the peak ("matched readout"), unless stated.

Significance marks. *** FDR < 0.001, ** < 0.01, * < 0.05, ns not significant. Tests are two-sided Mann–Whitney against a reference class, Benjamini–Hochberg corrected within each family of tests. With thousands of sites a tiny difference is "significant", so each comparison also shows an effect size (difference of medians with a bootstrap 95% CI, and Cliff's delta: about 0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large). Read the effect size before the stars.

Trust labels. ✓ Robust survives the checks below. ~ Plausible / partial real but small, or depends on a confound. ✗ Not supported no evidence, or indistinguishable from noise. ? Cannot judge yet data not available.

Part A. Where the data come from (QC)

These figures show how the site set, the model output and the runs themselves look before any hypothesis is tested. Each ends with what it means for how far the later results can be trusted.

A1. The site set

3,679 cardiomyocyte Fos sites: 2,907 Stable (79%) and 772 Dynamic, spread across the six dynamic binding patterns (79 to 210 sites each). Age and exercise labels are not independent: they come from the same three binding calls, so there are only seven patterns (for example every Age Up site is either Exercise Stable or Exercise Down). Chromosome counts follow chromosome size, and the Stable/Dynamic mix does not differ between chromosomes (chi-square p = 0.20; chrX has the highest Dynamic share, 34% of only 50 sites). Implication: class sizes are small (about 100 to 400), which limits the power of every class comparison. This site set is not the slides' (2,663 sites, 2,320 Stable).

A2. Site geometry

Dynamic sites sit in narrower peaks (median 700 vs 845 bp, Mann–Whitney p < 1e-10), but at a similar distance from TSSs (median 9,208 vs 8,752 bp, p = 0.14). About 15% of sites share their peak with another Fos site (about 8% of peaks hold two or more). Implication: peak width differs systematically between classes and also drives the peak-shuffle effect (Part C), which is why the class comparisons were adjusted for it.

A3. Native predicted accessibility, and how it compares with the slides

Predicted accessibility is strongly right-skewed: most sites are low (median 0.29) and a minority are very high. For Dynamic sites the means match the slides almost exactly (0.39 / 0.38 / 0.34 vs 0.39 / 0.42 / 0.34), which supports this pipeline reproducing the API model. Stable sites do not (0.79 / 0.76 / 0.46 vs 1.76 / 1.75 / 0.83); the slides' Stable set is a different, more accessible set of sites.

A4. Are the class labels real? Checking them against independent measured data

Comparison Class n sites Median measured log2FC
Age: log2(MAS/YS) Stable 2755 +0.027
Age: log2(MAS/YS) Age Up 364 +0.218
Age: log2(MAS/YS) Age Down 150 -0.044
Age: log2(MAS/YS) Neither YS nor MAS (= MAE only) 96 +0.083
Exercise: log2(MAE/MAS) Stable 2871 +0.000
Exercise: log2(MAE/MAS) Exercise Up 161 +0.112
Exercise: log2(MAE/MAS) Exercise Down 248 -0.082
Exercise: log2(MAE/MAS) Neither MAS nor MAE (= YS only) 85 +0.009

The classes come from TOBIAS footprint calls, not from accessibility, so measured accessibility is an independent check. The gains are clear and the losses are weak: Age Up sites gain accessibility with age (median log2 MAS/YS +0.22 vs +0.03 for Stable), as do Exercise Up sites (+0.11); Age Down and Exercise Down sites change in the expected direction but only slightly. Differences across classes are significant (Kruskal–Wallis p < 1e-10 (age) and p < 1e-10 (exercise)). Implication: the labels reflect real but modest accessibility shifts, so "Dynamic" classes are best read as footprint-defined, not as strongly differentially accessible.

A6. Does shuffling lower accessibility as expected? (the slides' QC)

Matched shuffle/readout Class Mean native ATAC Mean shuffled ATAC Sites that lose accessibility n
Motif (11 bp) Stable 0.789 0.62 74% 2907
Motif (11 bp) Dynamic 0.394 0.28 76% 772
170 bp Stable 0.756 0.24 97% 2907
170 bp Dynamic 0.381 0.17 94% 772
Peak Stable 0.463 0.23 82% 2907
Peak Dynamic 0.337 0.18 81% 772

Shuffling reduces accessibility on average everywhere, as on the slides. A 170 bp shuffle lowers the 170 bp readout in 97% of Stable sites, but a motif-only shuffle lowers the motif readout in only 74%: for about a quarter of sites it raises predicted accessibility, so the motif-only effect is small and heterogeneous. Implication: the shuffle experiment behaves as intended and the effect sizes are not an artefact of broken sequences.

A7. How many shuffle replicates are enough?

Replicates averaged Motif shuffle 170 bp shuffle Peak shuffle
1 0.447 0.181 0.357
3 0.225 0.099 0.191
5 0.149 0.066 0.126
7 0.097 0.042 0.082
9 0.050 0.020 0.040

With a single shuffle a site's effect is off by about 0.45 (motif), 0.18 (170 bp) and 0.36 (peak) log2 units; with 5 replicates it is about 0.15, 0.07 and 0.13. Motif and peak shuffles need the most replicates. Implication: 10 replicates is a sensible minimum; fewer would make single-site values unreliable, and even 10 leaves peak-shuffle per-site values noisy (this error is measured against the 10-replicate value itself, so the true error is somewhat larger).

A8. Does the compute hardware matter?

Measure Kruskal-Wallis p across GPU types Median (L40S) Median (A100) Median (H100)
Motif-shuffle effect 0.47 -0.602 -0.585 -0.498
170 bp-shuffle effect 0.32 -1.628 -1.614 -1.738
Peak-shuffle effect 0.22 -1.199 -1.222 -1.493
Native predicted ATAC 0.18 0.262 0.250 0.297

The private queue assigned chunks to L40S, A100 and one H100. Because sites are interleaved, each chunk is a random sample of all sites, so any GPU effect would show as a shift between colours. There is none (all p > 0.1; the H100 is a single chunk). Implication: mixing GPU types is safe.

Part B. Main results

B1. Does the model track real accessibility?

Track set Readout Spearman rho n
Mouse heart ATAC (CM) atac_motif 0.25 3365
Mouse heart ATAC (CM) atac_170 0.30 3365
Mouse heart ATAC (CM) atac_peak 0.40 3365
Mouse Patski ATAC (FB) atac_motif 0.03 3365

What it shows. The heart track predicts measured cardiomyocyte accessibility with a moderate rank correlation (the slides reported 0.49). The Patski (fibroblast-like) track is essentially uncorrelated with cardiomyocyte accessibility, as it should be. Trust: good enough to use the heart track as a proxy for cardiomyocyte sites; it is bulk heart tissue, not purified cardiomyocytes.

B2. What does shuffling do?

What it shows. Shuffling only the motif lowers accessibility at the motif by about 0.6 log2 units (roughly a third lost) and over the whole peak by about 0.3 (about a fifth lost). Shuffling 170 bp or the whole peak is far more damaging (about -1.8 log2 units locally, i.e. around 70% lost). Dynamic sites lose less than Stable sites in most cells. Trust: the ordering motif < 170 bp ≈ peak is robust. Peak shuffles are noisy per site (see B7).

B3. Stable vs Dynamic: is the difference real?

Dynamic sites have lower native accessibility and different peak widths, either of which could make their log2FC look smaller without any biological difference. Three checks:

Native quintile Native ATAC (median) n Stable n Dynamic Stable median Dynamic median Dyn - Stable FDR sig.
1 0.08 511 225 -1.20 -0.95 0.25 3.6e-07 ***
2 0.16 550 186 -1.92 -1.62 0.30 7.4e-06 ***
3 0.26 589 146 -2.38 -1.73 0.66 1.0e-10 ***
4 0.45 623 113 -2.24 -1.56 0.68 9.7e-06 ***
5 0.97 634 102 -1.46 -0.57 0.89 3.2e-12 ***
  • Stratification: the gap is present in all five accessibility quintiles (all FDR < 0.05), so it is not a floor effect of low-accessibility sites.
  • Permutation test (5,000 label shuffles): 170 bp p = 0.0002, peak p = 0.0002, motif p = 0.091. The 170 bp and peak differences are far outside the null; the motif one is not.
  • Independent track: repeating the test with the Patski ATAC track on the same sites gives 170 bp +0.16 (**), peak -0.03 (ns), motif -0.00 (ns). The 170 bp direction replicates; the others do not.

Trust: robust for the 170 bp shuffle; partial for the peak shuffle; not supported for the motif shuffle.

B4. Age, exercise and their combination

Each site carries three labels from the same binding calls: age class (YS vs MAS), exercise class (MAS vs MAE) and the full binding pattern. Every class is compared with its Stable reference, once raw and once adjusted for native ATAC and peak width (OLS with robust standard errors).

What it shows. At 170 bp every dynamic class loses about 0.45 to 0.6 log2FC less than Stable, and adjustment barely changes it. At the peak and motif widths, raw differences are small and the adjusted ones shrink toward zero. Between dynamic classes (the direct test of age vs exercise, and of up vs down):

Positive peak-width coefficient: wider peaks lose less accessibility per log2FC. Dynamic sites differ systematically from Stable sites in width and native accessibility, which is why the raw peak-shuffle gap shrinks after adjustment.

B5. RNA

What it shows. Predicted RNA barely moves when a distal AP-1 site or peak is shuffled (medians within about ±0.1), with the largest drops close to a TSS. ATAC and RNA effects correlate across sites (rho 0.19 to 0.24), so there is a weak coupling, but the RNA effects themselves are far smaller than the slides reported. Trust: not informative with these tracks; do not over-interpret.

Tier Class Motif shuffle 170 bp shuffle Peak shuffle

A: all sites Stable -0.61 -1.75 -1.25
B: measured peak and predicted >= 25th pct Dynamic -0.62 -1.55 -1.41
B: measured peak and predicted >= 25th pct Stable -0.64 -2.05 -1.51
C: B and rank-agreement within 1 SD Dynamic -0.61 -1.40 -1.41

What it shows. Effects get somewhat larger in the filtered sets (the model is more confident at accessible, well-predicted sites) and the Stable vs Dynamic gap at 170 bp stays. Trust: conclusions are not an artefact of poorly predicted sites; report all three tiers.

B7. How much is noise?

Shuffle Median effect Median replicate SD Median SE (10 reps) Sites with |effect| > 2 SE Sites with effect < -2 SE
Motif (11 bp) -0.59 0.67 0.21 67% 60%
170 bp -1.63 0.31 0.10 94% 94%
Peak -1.21 0.62 0.20 80% 77%

Replicate SD is the spread across the 10 shuffles of one site. The 170 bp effect is stable per site (SD about 0.3); the motif and peak effects scatter more (SD about 0.7 and 0.6). The median over thousands of sites is precise, but an individual site's peak-shuffle value should not be interpreted on its own. This is why 10 replicates were kept.

Part C. Further analyses

C1. How varied are the per-site effects?

The medians hide wide spread. For the motif shuffle, 19% of Stable sites gain accessibility and 30% lose more than half of it. For the 170 bp shuffle, 77% of Stable and 59% of Dynamic sites lose more than half. Implication: "AP-1 dependence" is a property of a subset of sites, not a uniform feature; class medians should be read together with these distributions.

C2. What drives the size of the effect?

Covariate (Spearman rho with the effect) Motif shuffle 170 bp shuffle Peak shuffle
Native predicted ATAC (peak) +0.03 -0.15 -0.52
Peak width +0.08 +0.09 +0.22
Distance to nearest TSS -0.12 -0.20 -0.02
TOBIAS footprint score -0.06 -0.34 -0.14

The peak-shuffle effect is mostly a function of how accessible and how wide the peak is (rho -0.52 and +0.22): there is more to lose in an accessible peak, and wider peaks lose less (the reason is not established here; one possibility is that a wide peak has more accessible sequence outside the site's immediate neighbourhood). The 170 bp effect has a U-shape across native accessibility (most loss in mid-high peaks, less at the very top, probably saturation), a clear dependence on distance to the TSS (rho -0.20) and on the footprint score (-0.34). The motif-only effect has only weak dependencies (|rho| ≤ 0.12). Implication: comparisons between groups that differ in accessibility or peak width must be adjusted, as was done in B3 and B4.

C3. Motif dependence vs context dependence

Site type n Share of Stable Share of Dynamic Median native ATAC Median peak width Median TSS distance
Context only 1722 49% 38% 0.27 808 9,590
Motif and context 979 28% 21% 0.25 770 11,470
Motif only 95 2% 4% 0.22 836 4,845
Neither 883 21% 36% 0.24 917 5,317

The two effects are positively related across sites (rho 0.35). Nearly half of Stable sites are "context only" (49%: the 170 bp shuffle hurts, the motif alone does not), 28% depend on both, and only 2.1% on the motif alone. Dynamic sites are far more often in the "neither" group (36% vs 21%); the composition differs between Stable and Dynamic (chi-square p < 1e-20). Implication: the AP-1 motif seldom works alone in this model; accessibility is largely set by the sequence around it. The 50% threshold is arbitrary, so use the proportions descriptively.

C4. Does footprint strength agree with the predicted dependence?

Outcome (vs footprint score) Sites Spearman rho CI lo CI hi n
Motif-shuffle effect Stable -0.06 -0.09 -0.02 2907
Motif-shuffle effect Dynamic -0.03 -0.11 +0.04 772
Motif-shuffle effect All -0.06 -0.10 -0.03 3679
170 bp-shuffle effect Stable -0.32 -0.35 -0.28 2907

In Stable sites, a stronger footprint goes with a larger predicted dependence on the 170 bp context (rho -0.32) and with higher predicted accessibility (+0.26); in Dynamic sites there is no relationship. This is independent experimental support for the model's picture of AP-1 sites. Caveat: footprint scores are computed from the same ATAC data that define accessibility, so strong footprints partly mean "very accessible", and the correlation is not fully independent evidence.

C5. Do two Fos sites in a peak buffer each other?

Shuffle n one motif n 2+ motifs Median (one) Median (2+) Raw diff CI lo CI hi FDR Adj. diff CI lo CI hi FDR
Motif (11 bp) 3126 553 -0.60 -0.59 0.01 -0.09 0.10 0.86 -0.01 -0.08 0.06 0.76
170 bp 3126 553 -1.63 -1.67 -0.04 -0.14 0.12 0.86 -0.02 -0.11 0.06 0.76
Peak 3125 553 -1.21 -1.25 -0.04 -0.12 0.07 0.86 -0.08 -0.14 -0.01 0.07

If a second motif compensated, the effect of shuffling one motif would be smaller in multi-motif peaks. It is not (differences about 0 at every width, all FDR ≥ 0.86). The adjusted peak-shuffle difference is -0.08 (FDR 0.07), not significant. Implication: no evidence for buffering, but only 553 sites are in multi-motif peaks, and each shuffle here edits one site’s window, not all motifs together.

10-30 kb +0.24 -0.66 -1.92 -1.25
>30 kb +0.22 -0.72 -2.06 -1.28

Sites within 2 kb of a TSS lie in much more accessible peaks (native ATAC 0.67 vs 0.22 beyond 30 kb) yet lose less from a 170 bp shuffle (-1.34 vs -2.06): promoter-proximal accessibility depends less on the AP-1 neighbourhood, distal enhancer-like sites more. The difference is large (p < 1e-29 at 170 bp). Implication: TSS distance is a real biological modifier of dependence and should be included when interpreting class differences.

Predicted native accessibility correlates weakly but consistently with MPRA activity (rho +0.25 heart, +0.19 Patski), and this holds in the replicated and TOBIAS-motif subsets. The predicted effect of shuffling does not track the MPRA at all (motif shuffle -0.00, full shuffle -0.02 with the Patski track; similar with heart). The MPRA delta is native minus shuffled, so agreement would appear as a negative correlation with the (negative) predicted log2FC; the confidence intervals exclude any correlation beyond about 0.06 in either direction. Possible reasons: the MPRA measures episomal enhancer activity of a 170 bp fragment, while the model predicts chromatin accessibility of the same sequence in its genomic context; the MPRA effects are small and noisy; and the fibroblast tracks are weak proxies. Implication: accessibility predicted by AlphaGenome should not be used as a proxy for the MPRA effect of disrupting an element.

D. What to trust

ClaimVerdictEvidence
Shuffling the 170 bp around a site removes far more predicted accessibility than shuffling the 11 bp motif alone✓ RobustMedian log2FC -1.75 (170 bp shuffle) vs -0.61 (motif shuffle) in Stable sites; 94% of sites show a 170 bp effect beyond 2 standard errors of their own replicate scatter.
Stable sites depend more on their 170 bp neighbourhood than Dynamic sites do✓ RobustDifference of medians +0.52 (95% CI +0.41 to +0.62), FDR 1.5e-34, permutation p = 0.0002. Holds in every native-accessibility quintile (all five FDR < 0.05), after adjusting for native ATAC and peak width (adjusted differences +0.46 to +0.61, all ***), and in every dynamic class. Direction replicates with the independent Patski ATAC track but is smaller (+0.16, **).
The direction of change (age up vs down, exercise up vs down) changes how much a site depends on its sequence✗ Not supportedDirectly comparing Age Up vs Age Down, and Exercise Up vs Exercise Down, shows no significant difference at 170 bp or peak level (smallest FDR 0.13). The large effects are all 'stably bound vs not', not up vs down.
Dynamic sites lose less accessibility than Stable sites when the whole peak is shuffled~ Plausible / partialRaw difference +0.19 (***), but small (Cliff's delta 0.10) and it mostly disappears after adjusting for native ATAC and peak width (adjusted +0.02 to +0.11; 1 of 6 class contrasts still FDR < 0.05). Not reproduced with the Patski track. Treat as a peak-width/accessibility effect.
Motif-only shuffling differs between Stable and Dynamic sites✗ Not supportedDifference +0.06 (Cliff's delta 0.05, negligible); permutation p = 0.091; not reproduced with the Patski track. A few individual classes (Age Down, Exercise Up, YS only, MAE only) differ by about 0.15 to 0.26 after adjustment, which is small relative to the replicate scatter.
Predicted RNA changes when an AP-1 site or peak is shuffled✗ Not supportedMedian RNA effects are about 0 (|log2FC| mostly < 0.1; largest -0.07 within 2 kb of a TSS). ATAC and RNA effects are correlated across sites (rho 0.19 to 0.24) but the RNA effect itself is tiny. Not informative with these tracks.
Predicted accessibility tracks measured snATAC accessibility~ Plausible / partialSpearman rho 0.40 (n = 3365) for the peak readout; lower for 170 bp and motif readouts. Good enough to be informative, not a precise predictor.
In a peak swap, the swapped-in sequence (not the location) sets accessibility✓ RobustSwapped vs donor native rho 0.75; vs recipient native 0.36. Caveat: only 4 recipients, so the 292 pairs are not independent (about 73 independent donors).
Inserting an AP-1 motif into a shuffled random background raises accessibility✗ Not supported+0.10 log2FC at the centre (p = 0.43); background ATAC is near zero, so the readout is at the floor. No usable signal.
Fibroblast-site results? Cannot judge yetFibroblast-site shuffles are not finished at the time of this report (the MPRA comparison is in C7). The fibroblast tracks available in the mouse model (Patski, embryonic fibroblast RNA) validated weakly against measured accessibility.
The TOBIAS binding classes correspond to real accessibility changes in the measured snATAC data~ Plausible / partialAge Up sites gain accessibility (median log2 MAS/YS +0.22 vs +0.03 for Stable), Exercise Up sites too (+0.11); the 'down' classes move the other way but only weakly (Age Down -0.04, Exercise Down -0.08). Kruskal-Wallis p < 1e-10 (age) and p < 1e-10 (exercise).
Predicted peak-shuffle loss mostly tracks how accessible and how wide a peak is✓ RobustSpearman rho -0.52 with native predicted accessibility and +0.22 with peak width; the motif-width effect depends on these much less (+0.03, +0.08).
Sites with stronger TOBIAS footprints are predicted to depend more on their 170 bp context~ Plausible / partialrho -0.32 in Stable sites (95% CI -0.35 to -0.28), none in Dynamic sites (+0.00). Independent data, but footprint scores come from the same ATAC data that define accessibility, so part of this is accessibility itself.
Several Fos motifs in one peak buffer each other (a second site makes a single shuffle matter less)✗ Not supportedNo difference: motif +0.01, 170 bp -0.04, peak -0.04 (FDR 0.86 to 0.86; n = 553 sites in multi-motif peaks).
Promoter-proximal sites depend less on their 170 bp context than distal sites✓ RobustMedian 170 bp effect in Stable sites: -1.34 within 2 kb of a TSS vs -2.06 beyond 30 kb (Mann-Whitney p < 1e-10); promoter-proximal peaks are also about 3x more accessible.
Most AP-1 sites that need their motif also need their surroundings; motif-only dependence is rare~ Plausible / partialOnly 2.1% of Stable sites lose more than half their accessibility from a motif shuffle without also losing it from a 170 bp shuffle (49% are context-only, 28% both). The thresholds (a 50% loss) are arbitrary, so treat the proportions as descriptive.
Predicted accessibility tracks MPRA enhancer activity~ Plausible / partialWeak but consistent positive correlation of native predicted ATAC with MPRA log2 alpha (heart +0.25, Patski +0.19; n = 1,653), reproduced in the replicated and TOBIAS-motif subsets.
The predicted accessibility loss from shuffling an element predicts its loss of MPRA activity✗ Not supportedNo correlation: motif shuffle rho -0.00 (95% CI -0.06 to +0.05, n = 1463), full shuffle -0.02. The intervals rule out anything larger than about |0.06|, so this is a real null, not a lack of power.
Results do not depend on which GPU ran a chunk; 10 replicates are enough✓ RobustChunk results are indistinguishable across L40S, A100 and H100 (Kruskal-Wallis p 0.18 to 0.47). Averaging 5 vs 10 replicates changes a site's effect by about 0.07 (170 bp), 0.15 (motif) and 0.13 (peak).

E. Open issues and next steps

  • Site set vs the slides. The TOBIAS table gives 3,679 CM Fos sites (2,907 Stable), not the slides' 2,663 (2,320 Stable). Our Dynamic native accessibility matches the slides, but our Stable sites are about half as accessible on average, and keeping our top 80% by predicted accessibility does not close the gap. The slides' Stable sites are a different set. Until the original selection is known, compare patterns, not absolute values.
  • Model equivalence. The slides were made with the AlphaGenome API; this run uses the PyTorch port with the same family of weights. The Dynamic-site match supports equivalence, but a direct check on the same sites through the API would settle it.
  • Status of the runs. The cardiomyocyte shuffle arm, the insertion jobs and the MPRA run are complete; the fibroblast-site shuffle array is still queued (nothing running yet), and the mutation arm (random, dinucleotide, core and flank edits) has not been run.
  • Fibroblasts. The mouse model has no fibroblast ATAC; Patski and embryonic-fibroblast RNA are weak proxies. The fibroblast shuffle run and the MPRA comparison will be added when they finish.
  • Motif-width effect is larger than in the slides (about -0.6 vs -0.12). Candidate causes are the motif interval used (here the 11 bp TOBIAS interval for both the shuffle and the readout) and the different Stable set; worth confirming the slides' definition.
Methods and files

Predictions: alphagenome-pytorch with model_all_folds weights, mouse organism, 131,072 bp window centred on the motif midpoint, mouse heart ATAC track (1 bp, mean over region), 10 uniform random shuffles per width. Stable = bound in YS, MAS and MAE; age class compares YS and MAS; exercise class compares MAS and MAE. Adjusted model: effect ~ class + log10(native ATAC over peak) + log10(peak width), HC3 robust SEs, normal-theory CIs. All CIs for medians are percentile bootstrap (1,000–2,000 resamples). Sites are treated as independent, but about 15% of sites share a peak with another site, so p-values are mildly optimistic; effect sizes and confidence intervals are the better guide. Tables: Analysis/cm/tables, Analysis/cm/stats; figures: Analysis/cm/figures; scripts: Scripts/22_shuffle_analysis.py, 24_class_stats.py, 23_insertion_analysis.py, 25_build_report.py.
